title: Up to 40 per cent of residential and on-street parking in inner Melbourne sits empty at night, and most street spaces are used by residents who already have off-street parking
oneLiner: The spillover fear meets the occupancy data.
body: Victoria's government cited up to 40 per cent of inner-Melbourne residential car parks sitting empty when it changed its rules, and Grattan's report found a similar share of on-street spaces vacant overnight, with most of the occupied ones used by residents who also have a garage or driveway. If the street is that underused, new residents' cars have somewhere to go.
contextBackground: This is the first systematic Australian evidence on the question the spillover objection turns on. It covers inner Melbourne; whether it generalises to middle suburbs is open.
contextDisagreement: Opponents say averages hide the streets that are full, and that it is those streets' residents who object. Supporters say that is an argument for permits on those streets, not for mandating basements everywhere.

evidenceItems.citation: Grattan Institute, Wasted space, May 2026 — on-street occupancy findings

claimItself.title: Without minimums, residents' cars spill onto surrounding streets and crowd out existing residents
claimItself.oneLiner: If the building does not house the cars, the street does.
claimItself.body: Residents of new developments will own cars at roughly the rate of their neighbours, whatever the building provides. Opponents of removal argue the predictable result is competition for kerbside space that existing residents regard as theirs.
